meta.title: Who really said "Writing is like sex. First you do it for love, then you do it for your friends, and then you do it for money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Virginia Woolf. Quote Investigator traces the quip to playwright Ferenc Molnár, quoted in George Jean Nathan's 1932 notebooks; the Woolf tag is recent.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Writing is like sex. First you do it for love, then you do it for your friends, and then you do it for money'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Woolf: Quote Investigator traces this to Ferenc Molnár, recorded by George Jean Nathan in 1932 as “Like a whore”. Molière and Woolf credits came later.

answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — probably Ferenc Molnár
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the quip to the Hungarian dramatist Ferenc Molnár. George Jean Nathan quotes him in The Intimate Notebooks of George Jean Nathan (Knopf, 1932) comparing his writing to a whore: done first for his own pleasure, then for his friends’, “and now—I do it for money.” QI calls the Woolf attribution “rather recent” and finds no source for the “Writing is like sex” wording in her work.

source.excerpt: We were sitting one morning two Summers ago, Ferenc Molnár, Dr. Rudolf Kommer and I, in the little garden of a coffee-house in the Austrian Tyrol. “Your writing?” we asked him. “How do you regard it?” Languidly he readjusted the inevitable monocle to his eye. “Like a whore,” he blandly ventured. “First, I did it for my own pleasure. Then I did it for the pleasure of my friends. And now—I do it for money.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ (2011, notes reformatted 2025) begins its chronology with Nathan’s 1932 Intimate Notebooks, where Molnár says “Like a whore”. QI concludes the quip was “probably first constructed by Ferenc Molnár around 1930.”

A 1958 Village Voice column by Nat Hentoff quoted crime writer Ed Lacy crediting “Writing is like prostitution” to Molière. QI ↗ calls this the earliest Molière attribution it has found and suggests Lacy may have misheard “Molnár”.
Wikiquote ↗ lists “Writing is like sex…” under Misattributed on its Virginia Woolf page and points to Quote Investigator and the Nathan passage.
The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ rates the line “Close but no cigar”. It credits Quote Investigator’s Molnár finding and notes that Woolf herself compared writing to prostitution.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator, which marks this citation “Verified on paper”. Wikiquote reproduces the same passage. The “Writing is like sex” version credited to Woolf is a later rewording with no identified source.

source.rightsNote: The “Writing is like sex” wording credited to Woolf has no identified author or first publication, so we assert no copyright status for it. The closest documented source, Nathan’s Intimate Notebooks, was first published in 1932. Under this site’s rules that date (1931 or later) is too recent to treat as public domain.

author.name: Ferenc Molnár
author.heading: About Ferenc Molnár
author.bio: Born Ferenc Neumann in Budapest, Molnár wrote The Paul Street Boys (1906) and stage hits including Liliom (1909), The Guardsman (1910) and The Swan (1920). He was known as a wit and raconteur. He left Europe for New York in January 1940 to escape the persecution of Hungarian Jews, and died there in 1952. Quote Investigator believes he probably first built this quip around 1930.

misattribution.heading: How the quip changed hands
misattribution.intro: One cynical joke about selling out has been passed between at least five famous names. Its wording drifted from “whore” to “prostitution” to the softened “sex” that now carries Woolf’s name.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ says the Woolf connection “appears to be rather recent” and gives a Goodreads listing as its example. It suggests a 1999 Modern Fiction Studies paper on Woolf’s prostitution metaphors may have encouraged the link.
The earliest Molière credit QI found is in Ed Lacy’s novel Breathe No More, My Lady, as quoted in the Village Voice in 1958. QI found no French or English source from Molière himself (QI ↗).
In his eleventh “Rule of Ethical Conduct” the painter put the saying in quotation marks without naming a source. It was later sometimes credited to him directly (QI ↗).
Secondhand accounts, including Leonard Nimoy’s memoir I Am Spock (1995), have the photographer reciting a version about his own career (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The first citation in QI’s chronology is Ferenc Molnár, quoted by George Jean Nathan in 1932: “Like a whore… now—I do it for money” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why Woolf’s name stuck
lead: Woolf did joke about writing for money in sexual terms, which may be why the misattribution feels plausible. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain points to a letter she wrote to Violet Dickinson on 8 June 1903: “I have sold my brains, which are my virtue. Never any lost woman felt so degraded as I do tonight” (Letters, vol. 1, p. 79). The Society credits the scholar Celia Marshik with noticing that Woolf compared prostitution and writing, and suggests this “may have led to the association of her name with similar sayings” (VWSGB ↗).

The neat three-step joke itself (love, then friends, then money) is Molnár’s, as far as Quote Investigator can trace. Later retellings in 1949, 1962, 1977 and in The Oxford Dictionary of Literary Quotations (1997) keep crediting him (QI ↗).
